title: Qualifiers and Limits
short: Words like usually, most and probably make a claim match its evidence.
trouble: Learners think qualifying a claim weakens it. An overstated claim is easier to knock down.

blocks.html: Toulmin’s qualifier answers the question “How sure are you?” Words like most, usually, often, probably, in many cases and for students at our school make a claim match its evidence.

blocks.name: wr-revise

opts.before: Phones ruin every student’s ability to focus.
opts.after: In our class survey, most students said phone alerts broke their focus during homework.

blocks.cap: Qualifying an overstated claim so it matches the evidence.

blocks.html: Claim exactly as much as your evidence shows. A survey of your class supports a claim about your class; a few cases support “often” or “sometimes,” not “always.”

An absolute claim (all, every, never, always) can be knocked down by a single counterexample. A qualified claim is harder to refute because it says only what the evidence shows. It also builds ethos: readers trust a writer who doesn’t overstate.

head: Evidence
Overstated
Matched
rows: A survey of 40 students in one school
Most students we surveyed want a later start.
Two cases of bikes stolen from unlocked racks
Every bike left at school will be stolen.
Unlocked bikes at our school have been stolen.
Several studies of sleep and grades
Students who sleep more tend to do better in school.
blocks.cap: The qualifier fits the size of the evidence.

blocks.title: Match the claim to the evidence
blocks.q: Evidence: “At our school, the three clubs that met at lunch lost half their members after lunch was shortened.” Which claim fits: (A) Shorter lunches destroy every club. (B) Shorter lunches may hurt clubs that meet at lunch. (C) Clubs are pointless.
steps: The evidence covers three clubs at one school.
A says “every club,” far beyond the evidence. C changes the subject.
B is limited to clubs that meet at lunch and says “may,” which fits a small sample.
blocks.a: B: it claims what three clubs at one school can show.

blocks.html: Thinking that qualifying a claim weakens it. An overstated claim is easier to knock down: one club that thrived after the change would refute “every club.” But don’t bury every sentence in hedges, either. Strunk (1918) warned against “tame, colorless, hesitating, non-committal language.” Qualify where the evidence is limited, then state the qualified claim firmly.
